subject: Svenska 3
title: Stylistics and linguistic variation
sourceSummary: Levels of style, how word choice and sentence structure create style, sociolect and register, and stylistically adapting your own text.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is written at a clearly FORMAL level of style?
questions.opener: Look at the word choice and sentence structure — are they everyday or elevated?
choices: Grejen är typ att vi måste fixa det här snabbt.
Härmed meddelas att ärendet kommer att behandlas vid nästa sammanträde.
Vi borde nog kolla på det där ganska snart, va?
Kan vi typ ta det där sen liksom?
questions.explanation: The formal sentence uses officialese ("härmed meddelas" ["hereby notified"], "ärendet" ["the matter"], "sammanträde" ["meeting"]) and a complete, impersonal sentence structure. The other options contain spoken-language markers such as "typ", "liksom" and "va" (roughly "like", "sort of" and "right?"), which signal an informal/everyday style.

questions.prompt: What is typical of an EVERYDAY (speech-like) level of style in writing?
questions.opener: Consider how you actually talk with friends, compared with how you write an official letter.
choices: Long, complex subordinate clauses and the passive voice
Filler words ("typ", "liksom" — roughly "like", "sort of"), everyday words, and shorter, simpler sentences
Only technical terms and Latin expressions
A total absence of pronouns
questions.explanation: Everyday style is characterised by speech-like features such as filler words, simpler word choice and shorter sentences. Long subordinate clauses, passive constructions and technical terms instead belong to a more formal or academic style.

questions.prompt: An author writes "The wind whispered through the branches of the trees" instead of "It was blowing gently". Which stylistic device is used to create a more literary style?
questions.opener: What is attributed to the wind here that is really a human trait?
choices: Concretisation of an abstract concept
Turning the sentence into the passive voice
A shift to a spoken-language style
Personification — the wind is attributed a human action (whispering)
questions.explanation: Having the wind "whisper" is personification: a human trait (whispering) is attributed to something non-human, which gives a more vivid, literary style compared with the neutral version "it was blowing gently".

questions.prompt: How do sentence length and clause structure often affect the stylistic impression of a text?
questions.opener: Compare the feeling of several short, clipped sentences with a single long, branching sentence.
choices: Sentence length has no bearing on the stylistic impression, only word choice matters
Short sentences always give a more formal style than long ones
Short, simple sentences can give a terse or intense impression, while long, complex sentences with subordinate clauses often give a more expository or elevated impression
Long sentences are automatically a sign of poor writing ability
questions.explanation: Sentence structure contributes strongly to style: short, clipped sentences often create drive or tension, while longer sentences with subordinate clauses signal thoughtfulness, complexity or formality. Long sentences are not in themselves a quality problem, just one stylistic device among several.

questions.opener: Distinguish this from dialect, which is tied to geography.
choices: A regional variant of the language linked to a particular place or part of the country
A way of using language linked to a social group, e.g. based on age, occupation or social class
Another word for formal written language
A language spoken in another country
questions.explanation: A sociolect is a linguistic variant linked to a social group — e.g. youth slang, a particular professional jargon, or a social class — as distinct from a dialect, which is instead tied to geographical origin.

questions.prompt: What is meant by REGISTER in a linguistic context?
questions.opener: Consider how the same person can speak differently depending on the situation, not depending on which group they belong to.
choices: The linguistic variant a speaker or writer chooses depending on the situation and recipient, e.g. a formal register at work and an informal one among friends
A list of all the words in a language
Another word for sociolect, fully interchangeable
The dialect a person was born with and can never change
questions.explanation: Register is about the same person deliberately switching linguistic style depending on the context — formal at an official meeting, informal among friends. Unlike sociolect, which is linked to group membership, register is a situational adaptation each individual makes.

questions.prompt: Rewrite the sentence "Vi måste typ fixa det där problemet asap, annars blir det kaos" at a formal level of style suitable for an official letter.
questions.opener: Replace spoken-language words and make the sentence structure more complete and impersonal.
questions.answer: Problemet bör åtgärdas skyndsamt, då underlåtenhet att göra så riskerar att medföra allvarliga konsekvenser.
steps: Remove spoken-language filler words such as "typ" ("like") and abbreviations such as "asap".
Replace everyday expressions with more formal equivalents: "fixa" ("sort out") → "åtgärda" ("address/rectify"), "kaos" ("chaos") → "allvarliga konsekvenser" ("serious consequences").
Make the sentence structure more complete and written in style, preferably with a subordinate clause instead of "annars" ("otherwise").
Tone down the personal "vi" ("we") in favour of a more impersonal construction, e.g. the passive voice.

questions.prompt: Summarise levels of style, sociolect, register and key stylistic devices.
questions.opener: Keep apart what depends on situation and what depends on group membership.
questions.answer: Levels of style: formal (officialese, impersonal) · neutral · informal/everyday (speech-like, filler words) · Sociolect: language use linked to a social group (age, occupation, class) · Register: the level of style a person deliberately chooses depending on the situation · Sentence structure: short sentences give terseness/drive, long ones give thoughtfulness/formality · Personification: human traits attributed to non-human phenomena · Word choice determines the stylistic impression just as much as grammar.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is written at a clearly NEUTRAL level of style, neither markedly formal nor everyday?
questions.opener: Look for the sentence that has neither officialese nor speech-like filler words.
choices: Mötet är planerat till klockan tio på torsdag. ("The meeting is scheduled for ten o'clock on Thursday.")
Härmed inkallas ni till sammanträde klockan tio på torsdagen den nionde. ("You are hereby summoned to a meeting at ten o'clock on Thursday the ninth.")
Vi ses typ tio-ish på torsdag, okej? ("See you like ten-ish on Thursday, okay?")
Torsdag tio, fixar du det? ("Thursday ten, can you sort that?")
questions.explanation: "Mötet är planerat till klockan tio på torsdag" is factual and clear without being either officialese-formal or speech-like everyday, which makes it an example of a neutral level of style. The other options clearly lean toward either the formal or the everyday end.

questions.prompt: A text describes rain as having "fallit som nålar mot marken" ("fallen like needles against the ground"). Which stylistic device is used here?
questions.opener: The word "like" ("som") signals a comparison between two different things.
choices: Simile (a comparison using a word like "like")
Metonymy
Euphemism
Anaphora
questions.explanation: A simile explicitly compares two different things using a comparing word such as "like" — here the raindrops are compared to needles. Metonymy would instead involve replacing a word with a closely related concept.

questions.prompt: A doctor uses technical jargon with colleagues but explains the same information with simpler words for a patient. Is this an example of sociolect or register?
questions.opener: Consider whether this is about which group the doctor belongs to, or a deliberate choice depending on the situation.
choices: Register, since the doctor deliberately switches style depending on the situation and recipient
Sociolect, since the doctor belongs to a professional group
Neither register nor sociolect
Both register and sociolect in exactly the same way
questions.explanation: This is an example of register, since the same doctor deliberately switches linguistic style depending on who they are talking to. The doctor's technical jargon itself could be seen as a sociolect linked to the profession, but the actual switching between situations is register.

questions.prompt: Which of the following word pairs most clearly shows a difference in level of style, from formal to everyday?
questions.opener: A pair should consist of two different words with the same meaning but different stylistic value.
choices: "Erhålla" ("to obtain") compared with "få" ("to get")
"Hus" ("house") compared with "hus" ("house")
"Springa" ("to run") compared with "springa" ("to run")
"Bil" ("car") compared with "bil" ("car")
questions.explanation: "Erhålla" is a clearly formal word while "få" is its everyday equivalent, which makes the pair a good example of a stylistic-level difference. The other pairs compare the same word with itself and therefore show no stylistic difference at all.

questions.prompt: Which type of text would you normally expect to have a high, formal level of style?
questions.opener: Think about which text has the highest demands for precision and impersonality.
choices: A court verdict or a government decision
A text message between close friends
A chat on a social forum for teenagers
A spoken comment during a football match among friends
questions.explanation: A court verdict or a government decision requires high precision and an impersonal, formal style to avoid misunderstanding. Text messages, chats among teenagers, and comments among friends instead allow a much more everyday level of style.

questions.prompt: What is a typical difference between a sociolect linked to young people and one linked to an older generation?
questions.opener: Think about what tends to vary between generations' ways of speaking.
choices: Differences in vocabulary, slang expressions, and sometimes pronunciation that signal belonging to the respective group
There are never any differences between generations' language use
Sociolects never change over time
Sociolect is only about written language, never spoken language
questions.explanation: Different generations' sociolects often differ in vocabulary, slang expressions and sometimes pronunciation, which signals belonging to a particular age group. Sociolects also change over time and occur mainly in spoken language, although traits can show up in writing too.

questions.prompt: Why might an author deliberately mix formal and everyday levels of style within the same text?
questions.opener: Think about what contrasts in language can be used to show.
choices: To create contrast, for example to mark a class difference between characters or for comic effect
It is always a writing mistake that should be avoided
It automatically makes the text harder to understand for no purpose
Mixed levels of style are forbidden in fiction
questions.explanation: Deliberately mixing levels of style can create contrast, for example to mark differences between characters or for comic effect, and is a common and accepted stylistic device in fiction rather than a mistake.
